01
Act one · Provenance
Where the numbers came from
Pragathi P · 2314446

Rule one: no number gets typed twice.

Before a single forecast, we had to get three years of audited Ind AS statements out of PDF and into one consistent database. That pipeline is documented in the workbook itself — five prompts, five purposes, on the AI Prompt Log tab. We logged it so anyone can re-run it and land on our numbers.

What we refused to let AI do
  • Infer a figure. Step 1 says “Do not reclassify, round, or infer any figure at this stage.” Extraction is transcription, not judgement.
  • Copy a subtotal. Step 4 forces Gross Profit, EBITDA, EBIT, Total Assets and Total Equity to be recomputed from components, never pasted.
  • Pass QA on its own say-so. Step 5 is a reviewer prompt that must reconcile back to the source PDF and report the exact figure and location of any break.
The four QA gates the raw data had to clear
(a) Total Assets = Total Liabilities + EquityPASS
(b) CF closing cash = BS cashPASS
(c) P&L Net Income = CF opening linePASS
(d) Every subtotal recomputesPASS

These four became checks 1, 2, 4 and 8 on the live Validation Panel — Prisha picks that up in Act 3.

Act 1 · Provenance Pragathi P · 2314446

The crore trap — and why it didn't get us.

Waaree changed reporting units mid-stream. FY23 and FY24 are published in ₹ million. FY25 is published in ₹ crore. Paste all three into one row without thinking and your model reports that India's largest module maker shrank by 87% in its best year ever. Click the toggle.

The rule we wrote into Step 3
// AI Prompt Log · Step 3 — Unit Normalization "Convert every FY2024-25 value to ₹ million using 1 crore = 10 million (multiply by 10). …add a one-line audit note confirming the conversion factor applied."

Every FY25 figure in the workbook carries that ×10. The audit note is the reason we can prove it.

Why it mattered downstream

Get this wrong and it isn't one bad cell — it's the entire forecast. FY25 is the anchor year for almost every driver we set: the 30/93/78 working-capital days, the 7.15% interest rate, the 22.7% capex intensity, the ₹95,953 mn equity base the DCF discounts back to.

A unit error in FY25 doesn't produce a wrong answer. It produces a wrong model.

The honesty line — what we deliberately did not do

There is no plug row on our balance sheet. No “other assets — balancing figure”. The one adjusting line that exists, Cash Flow · row 33 “Effect of FX & Other Adjustments”, is historical only — it reconciles the audited opening/closing cash we transcribed, and it is set to zero in every forecast year.

// Cash Flow · C33 (history) — reconciles audited cash =C36-C34-C35 // Cash Flow · F33:J33 (forecast) — hard zero 0

In the forecast, cash has nowhere to hide. It has to fall out of the cash flow statement correctly or the model breaks.

Act 3 · Architecture & integrity Prisha Das · 2311356

The golden rule: cash is the plug, and cash is the only plug.

This is the single design decision that makes a three-statement model honest. Nothing is forced to balance. Every account is derived, and whatever is left over lands in cash — which then gets written back to the balance sheet. If any link is wrong, the check breaks. Follow the loop.

The closing link — Balance Sheet · F7
='Cash Flow Statement'!F36

Balance-sheet cash is cash-flow closing cash. Not a copy, not a hardcode — a live reference. And cash-flow closing cash is itself =F35+F34+F33, i.e. opening + net change. The circle closes.

And the opening link — Cash Flow · G35
=F36  // this year's opening = last year's closing

Check 10 on the Validation Panel exists purely to police this one line across all eight columns.

Why we avoided circularity — and didn't need iteration

The classic trap is interest on average cash: cash → interest → net income → cash. We sidestepped it deliberately.

  • Other income is a % of revenue (2.5%), not a yield on the cash balance. Revenue is known before cash is, so there is no loop.
  • Interest expense is a rate on debt (7.15% × interest-bearing debt), and debt is held flat — so it never depends on the cash the model is trying to solve for.

Result: the workbook computes in a single pass. No iterative calculation, no circular-reference warning, no hidden convergence hiding an error.

Act 3 · Architecture & integrity Prisha Das · 2311356

We didn't want to claim the model ties out — we wanted the workbook to prove it on every recalculation. So the Validation Panel tab computes every tie automatically, and a master cell goes red the instant any one of them fails.

05
Act five · Schedules & valuation
From roll-forwards to a share price
Swastik Jena · 2311371

Four roll-forwards do all the real work.

A balance-sheet line can't just be “last year × growth”. It has to be built. Each of these schedules opens where last year closed, adds what happened, and hands the closing figure to the balance sheet.

① PP&E — gross block, not net
// Depreciation Capex Forecast Opening gross F15 = E18 (+) Capex F16 = F7*F10 // revenue × capex% Closing gross F18 = F15+F16-F17 Depreciation F22 = F18/F12 // SLM, 15-yr life Net PP&E F26 = F18-F24

We seeded the FY25 gross block as =E12*E12 — depreciation × useful life — then reverse-solved accumulated depreciation as =E18-'Balance Sheet'!E16. That's why depreciation grows with the asset base, not with revenue.

② Working capital — days, not percentages
// Working Capital Forecast Receivables F19 = F7/365*F11 // revenue, DSO 30 Inventory F20 = F8/365*F12 // CoS, DIO 93 Payables F22 = F8/365*F13 // CoS, DPO 78

Receivables run off revenue; inventory and payables run off cost of sales. Getting that base right is the difference between a working-capital schedule and a guess. Historical days are back-solved live — C11 ='Balance Sheet'!C9/C7*365 — so you can see 186 inventory days in FY23 collapse to 93 by FY25.

③ Debt — flat, and interest priced off it
// Debt Forecast Interest-bearing F20 = F12+F17+'Balance Sheet'!F41 Interest expense F22 = F21*F20 // 7.15% × 21,261.3

Note the base includes lease liabilities — that's how we got a 7.15% rate that actually reconciles to FY25's reported ₹1,520.9 mn finance cost.

④ Equity — retained earnings roll
// Shareholders Equity Forecast Opening G17 = F21 (+) NI G18 = G7 (-) Divs G19 = -G9 // = NI × payout%, payout = 0 Closing G21 = G17+G18+G19+G20

Zero payout is not an oversight — Waaree paid ₹2.65 mn and ₹5.32 mn of dividends on ₹5 bn and ₹12.7 bn of profit, then nothing in FY25. A 0.05% historical payout rounds to zero.

Capex, depreciation and net PP&E · ₹ million · one axis

Act 5 · Schedules & valuation Swastik Jena · 2311371

Before you argue with the answer, argue with the inputs.

A single DCF number is a bad argument. So here is the honest version: target price at every sensible combination of WACC and terminal growth, computed live off the same engine. Hover any cell.

Target price ₹/share · WACC (rows) × terminal growth (columns)
What the grid actually says
  • Across the whole plausible range the target lands roughly ₹660 – ₹1,500.
  • Not one cell reaches ₹2,923. To get there you'd need terminal growth pushing toward WACC — i.e. assuming Waaree compounds at close to its discount rate forever.
  • That's the finding. It isn't that our model is bearish; it's that the price requires an assumption we can't defend from three years of audited statements.
Where we'd push back on ourselves
  • Other investing activities are zero in the forecast — historically −₹13 bn to −₹36 bn a year. That's why cash compounds to ₹1,48,181 mn. It flatters the balance sheet, not the DCF (FCFF excludes it).
  • Zero payout is faithful to history but unusual for a listed company. Toggle 40% on Saikruthi's slider and cash halves — equity value doesn't move, which is the correct behaviour.
  • β = 1.2 is a judgement, not a regression. It's the single input with the most leverage on the answer — hence this grid.
Act 5 · Schedules & valuation Swastik Jena · 2311371

The call: SELL — and not because the business is bad.

The verdict, as written on the Summary tab

“The stock is priced like Waaree is still in its hyper-growth phase, and the numbers on this model say it isn't anymore. Investors are paying multiples you'd expect from a company still doubling revenue every year or two. But the growth story here is one of deceleration, not repetition — the model has that clearly tapering off by FY30.”

“Run the DCF and the fair value comes out well below the current share price, and the call, for now, is SELL. Not because the business is broken — it's a well-run, conservatively financed company with almost no debt — but because the price already assumes a version of Waaree that the forecast doesn't think shows up.”

Even if you hand the market our entire five-year forecast for free, today's price is still 21.5× the earnings we get to in FY30. That is the whole argument in one row.

The one caveat we'd state out loud

Waaree's audited statements disclose consolidated totals only, so revenue is modelled as a single growth line. We allocate it to segments using the FY25 mix (modules 89.7%, EPC 10.8%) for disclosure, but no segment-level forecast drives the model.

If you remember one thing about how this was built
1

Historicals are transcribed from audited PDFs and logged, not scraped from a data terminal.

2

Every balance-sheet line rolls forward through its own schedule.

3

Cash is the only plug — and ten automated checks police it.

4

Change any blue cell and the whole thing reflows and still balances.
